h1: Introducing Primefold - Saypien is becoming Primefold
h2: Ask your data. Get the answer.
h4: Why we changed: clarity, consistency, and a stronger narrative
Our name isn’t arbitrary. It’s geological, strategic, and a bit poetic.
Primefold XI unlocks experience intelligence: Chat in. Survey out. Decisions on.
p: We‘ve transformed. That’s the process of metamorphosis: It’s a transformation that happens in stages, where the core stays continuous, but the form evolves until it matches what you’ve grown into. And here we are: shifted, merged and outgrown. As our vision grew and our platform matured, our old identity stopped reflecting the full picture, and it was time to shed it.

Starting now, you’ll see us act more visibly with a clearer system and a stronger way to express what we’re building. This is not a change of direction. It’s a more precise and future proof way to communicate what we’ve become and where we’re going next.
Saypien is becoming Primefold.Saights is becoming Primefold XI.
We’re closing one chapter and opening the next with Primefold as the umbrella brand, and Primefold XI as the first platform built within that structure.

Over time, our work evolved beyond a single product label or category. We’re not “just” doing surveys. We’re not “just” doing analytics. We’re building technology that helps organizations turn scattered signals into clear decisions, reliably, repeatedly, and across teams.

The Primefold brand gives us clearer positioning for what we already are, a product narrative that’s easier to understand and explain, and consistency as we expand the Primefold platform family over time.

In geology, a fold forms when layers of rock are compressed by tectonic forces, creating structures that reveal history and composition. Each layer tells a story: different eras, different contexts. Under pressure, they bend together into something readable, something with shape and structure.

That’s what happens inside every modern organization. Data accumulates in layers. Signals live in different tools and teams. Context gets fragmented. Important truths get buried under operational noise.

Primefold is our commitment to compress these layers into a single intelligible structure, so what’s scattered becomes readable, and what’s ambiguous becomes actionable. Most tools dig vertically into one layer, one channel, one dataset, one dashboard. Our approach is different. We fold horizontally across layers, connecting fragments into a coherent view.
When we say experience intelligence, we don’t mean analytics about experience. We mean an operating system for experience decisions.

Companies receive signals from many places: customer feedback, surveys, behavior, sentiment, and trends. Most of it is scattered and difficult to interpret. Primefold XI brings these signals together and turns them into a clear, structured view of what is happening, why it is happening, and what to do next.

In practice, Primefold XI helps teams capture signals across channels, structured and open text, connect the dots across teams and touchpoints, turn noise into themes and decision-ready priorities, surface drivers and emerging issues early, and translate insight into next actions teams can align on.
It’s built for momentum: clarity that actually leads to action.
Primefold is the umbrella brand because our ambition goes beyond one platform. Over time, we’re building a family of systems, each grounded in the same philosophy.
Make scattered data readable. Make decisions easier. Make action faster.Primefold XI is the first expression of that umbrella in the market, and it will continue to lead the way.
If you’d like a short walkthrough of what’s changing and what it means for you, please reach out anytime. We’re here to support you and will make sure the transition feels simple on your side.
And if you’d like to explore Primefold XI early, you can already join the waitlist to get updates and early access as we roll things out.

h1: NAS Invest Turned Tenant Insight Into Tenant Strength
h2: It Felt Too Easy to Be True
Outcome: From Feedback Collection to Tenant Strength
Ask your data. Get the answer.
p: A story of light technology, deep understanding, and real world change

In Frankfurt’s skyline, NAS Invest operates some of the city’s most defining properties. Vertical ecosystems where tenants expect more than square meters. They expect experience, responsiveness, and a building that listens. In a competitive market, asset managers must not only maintain assets, but actively understand the people inside them.
The question was simple, yet unsolved: How do you give thousands of tenants a direct way to communicate with a handful of asset managers and still act fast enough for it to matter?

The project landed with an asset manager already stretched thin, with no background in tenant engagement or market research. He expected long survey drafts, slow iteration loops, and days of manual analysis. Instead, Primefold XI flipped the workload: surveys built in minutes, alignment in a day, and insights available live. Technology designed to remove effort, not add it.
Primefold XI’s AI guided every step, from structure and logic to branding, incentives, and QR distribution. It didn’t feel like learning a tool. It felt like working with a co pilot.
Still, the doubts were real. Would tenants respond? Would the insights be meaningful? Can an agentic system be trusted for something as human as sentiment?
Historically, tenant feedback at NAS, like in most real estate organizations, lived in fragments. Scattered notes, isolated complaints, and improvised surveys that never produced a coherent picture.

Within just a week, more than 100 tenants responded. Not because NAS suddenly became a research organization, but because the process finally fit into real operations. Setup was simple, distribution frictionless, and the real shift came when Sunday, Primefold XI’s AI co pilot, turned incoming feedback into something the team could use immediately.

What used to be messy and subjective became structured. Open text stopped being “a pile of comments” and became clear themes in seconds. Recurring frustrations, hidden delights, emerging needs, and silent risks were organized into a view you could act on.
Primefold XI unlocks experience intelligence. Not analytics about experience, but an operating system for experience decisions.

In this case, NAS had signals everywhere and clarity nowhere. Tenant sentiment existed across buildings and touchpoints, but it wasn’t connected in a way that supported decisions. Primefold XI folded separate layers into one decision ready view that made three things visible at once:
What is happening across buildings and tenant groups
Why it is happening, by surfacing the strongest drivers in tenants’ own language
What to do next, by translating themes into prioritized actions the team can align on
This is the “Primefold” principle in action: separate layers compressed into a structure that reveals meaning fast.

Open questions covered the end to end tenant experience, from workspace and building services to neighborhood context and future needs. What came back was not noise, but clarity. Primefold XI surfaced the underlying emotional structure of the buildings, including:
Service quality and operational friction (canteen experience, maintenance gaps)
Connection and communication needs (shared spaces, clearer tenant updates)

NAS didn’t just review the feedback, they operationalized it. Together with Sunday, they translated insight into priorities and moved quickly. Within three weeks, a new canteen was approved, repairs were executed, and tenant communication was upgraded.

With Primefold XI, NAS moved beyond collecting feedback to understanding tenants at scale. Responses across buildings were consolidated into a single unified view. Patterns became visible, sentiment could be benchmarked, and the highest impact actions became easier to identify and execute.
Primefold XI did not just help NAS listen. It gave every building a voice and gave the team the speed to act while it still mattered.

p: Last month we told you something was coming. Now it's here.

When we shared the new Insights Hub, we said two things were still on the roadmap: a new Design page and a fresh take on Reports. We wanted to give each of them their own moment instead of rushing them out the door. That moment is now.
Let’s have a look at how this is impacting you in your work with Primefold XI!
The Design page is where your surveys get their look and feel. Until now, every change went live instantly, with no easy way back. That's changed.
Theme updates now save as a draft first. Nothing goes live until you hit publish.
Every change sits in draft state until you're ready
Your live surveys stay untouched until then
Design work also isn't a straight line, so we added full history. You can undo and redo any step, and see exactly which colors and photos changed along the way.
A few smaller improvements round it out:
Smoother chat flow with better error handling
Clearer previews when Sunday generates a theme for you
Chat history is saved, so you can pick up right where you left off

Reports got the deeper rework. The goal was simple: less noise, more signal, and a clear sense of what to actually do with what you're seeing.
We started with length. Reports are now capped at fifteen pages. That constraint forced something good: every page has to earn its place!

From there, the intelligence got sharper. Reports now lean on more charts and graphics, and they vary them, so a report reads like a story being told rather than the same bar chart on repeat. More importantly, the AI now looks for real findings, the kind that only surface when you connect the answers across several questions. Not "here's what people said," but "here's what it means when you put these answers together."

And it doesn't stop at insight. Reports now make concrete suggestions for what to do next. Things like "focus on this age segment, because those customers are both highly satisfied and have real budget to spend," or "give customers outside the big cities a better way to order, because of what the data shows." Findings you can move on, not just nod at.
We also made sure the generated slides sit properly on the PDF pages, so everything looks as polished printed as it does on screen. And we fixed a list of bugs while we were in there!

Two chapters, both delivered. The Insights Hub became proactive. Design became something you can shape without fear. h1: How we built Sunday's survey design agent
h2: What Sunday’s design agent actually does
Ask your data. Get the answer.
p: Creating a survey should not mean rebuilding your brand from scratch.

That was the thought that kept coming up inside Primefold, long before a single line of code was written for what would become our Survey Design Agent. Teams would spend hours picking colors, hunting down the right shade of blue from a brand guideline PDF, resizing a logo, second guessing a font, all before they'd written a single question. The survey itself, the part that actually mattered, kept getting pushed to the end.
We wanted to flip that order, so we taught Sunday to design.
Every feature at Primefold starts with the same question: How does this save our customer time?
Before developing the new design feature, we had a more specific question: Where is the gap between having an idea and seeing it become a finished, on-brand survey?

Design kept showing up as that gap. It wasn't that people didn't care about design. It's that designing was taking the time the questions needed. The team started sketching what it would look like if Sunday simply understood a brand the way a designer would, by looking at it, rather than asking a customer to manually translate their brand into settings, sliders and hex codes.

Sarah, one of the engineers behind the feature, remembers the goal starting somewhere simpler: "Our general goal was to really simplify the editor so it's easier to use. There are less options, but the idea was to create an editor that produces a consistent design throughout the survey, with better navigation between the intro, survey, and outro pages as well. We wanted to enable users to have a few, important customization controls for a streamlined editing experience that still creates beautiful surveys with the same design all the way through."
You don't need a brand guideline to start. Sunday works with what you have:
1. Your website. Hand Sunday the URL and it reads your visual identity off the page: colors, typography and logo, applied to your survey automatically. No manual matching, no guesswork.
2. A sentence. No site to point at? Describe the look you want in the AI toolbar and Sunday builds the theme from that. Refining a theme you already have works the same way.
3. A brand you like. Name it and Sunday pulls what it needs from the web, then adapts your survey thoughtfully to the design rather than just copying it.

In each case, the outcome is the same: a survey that feels like a natural extension of your website or brand, not a bolt on form. You spend less time on layout decisions and more time on the questions that actually drive insight. And manual, hands on design is always still there if that's how you like to work. Sunday is a shortcut, not a requirement.
Teaching an AI Agent to see a brand and make good design judgment turned out to be far harder than teaching it to copy a hex code.

"I really enjoy working on UI based features that you can see and experience, and trying to design it to give users the best possible experience," Sarah says. "The most challenging part was overhauling the whole editor from the ground up without endangering or changing existing, live surveys in any way. It was very tricky to still support the old data structures while simultaneously creating new ones, and I was very relieved that we had a successful release without any issues on live surveys."

What that meant in practice: getting from "extract some colors" to "apply them in a way that looks intentional" required a lot of iteration, a lot of unflattering survey screenshots on Slack and a fair amount of arguing about what "on brand" even means when the AI only has a website to go on, all while keeping every survey already running out in the world completely untouched.

The distance we wanted to collapse is the one between “I have an idea for a survey” and “I have a branded survey ready to send.” Picking a shade of blue was never the part that needed you. Deciding what to ask, and why, always was. That is what customer obsession means to us in practice. We're not telling you how your survey should look. We're giving you a faster way to make it look like exactly what you already had in mind.
All of this is live in Sunday's AI toolbar. Point it at your website, describe what you want or name a brand you admire, and see what comes back.
Next up: Our Shopify integration is live – get to know how it works, why we built it and how you can implement it on your post purchase page.

Primefold XI replaces that whole chain with one conversation. Sunday is who you have it with.

Inside Primefold XI, Sunday is who you talk to, instead of digging through layers of data yourself. Not a chatbot bolted onto a dashboard or a search bar with a friendly font. Sunday is there from your first login, through building your survey, designing how it looks, and understanding what respondents actually said.

Sunday is AI, built into the product, not added on top. Under the hood, it's our intelligence layer: connected to your workspace, your data and your history. That's why answers are data-backed and specific to your company, not just generic output pulled from nowhere.

Most survey tools start with a blank canvas and a question type picker. With Sunday, you start with a sentence.

Tell Sunday what you want to learn. Sunday drafts the questions, arranges the pages, and gets a research-grade survey ready to publish. No blank-page problem. No wondering if your rating scale makes sense. You still decide what to ask and why; Sunday removes everything standing between that decision and a finished survey.
This is where a lot of survey tools quietly cost you the most time: matching colors, hunting for the right shade of blue, resizing a logo, before you've even shipped the thing that matters.

Sunday skips that. Point Sunday at your website, describe the look you're after, or name a brand you like, and Sunday builds a matching theme in the survey editor's Design tab. Ask Sunday what's changing in your numbers, what's driving a pattern or what you should do next. Sunday doesn’t just give you charts that make you question what happened, or raw numbers you have to interpret alone. Instead, Sunday surfaces summaries, themes, sentiment, and delivers decision-ready reports based on live analysis.

The point isn't that each of these functionalities is clever on its own. It's that they're the same Sunday, in the same conversation, from the first question you write to the last response you read. Nothing you build gets handed off to a different tool halfway through. Nothing gets lost in translation between "what we asked" and "what we learned."
That's the shift Primefold XI is built around: Experience Intelligence – an intelligence that works alongside you, instead of a static dashboard that waits for you to come looking.

Surveys are where most teams start, but the conversation doesn't have to stop at the questionnaire. As your data grows, Sunday connects your responses, surfaces patterns, and helps you see the fuller picture. Most teams only discover how deep that goes once they're in.

Companies sit on signals from customers, employees, and users every day. Most of those signals never become decisions. Sunday exists to shorten that distance: from a question to clarity you can act on.

Your data stays yours. Sunday runs on infrastructure hosted in Germany, built GDPR-ready from the ground up. Every recommendation Sunday gives you is traceable back to the responses behind it. No black-box reasoning, nothing you have to take on faith.

Reading about Sunday only gets you so far. The fastest way to understand it is to open a new survey and just start talking. Ask for what you want to learn, point Sunday at your website, and see how quickly a blank page turns into something you can send.

h1: Primefold RI is here: Real Estate Intelligence, built to grow asset value
h2: What you can do with it
What it looked like at NAS Invest
Ask your data. Get the answer.
p: Real estate runs on documents. A single asset carries its leases, its rent roll and a decade of amendments, drafted by different people in different systems. All of these sit in scattered silos.
None of that is unusual, and none of it is anyone's fault. It is simply how an asset gets documented. And it's a problem.
Real estate teams don’t lack data. They lack time to use it.

The answer to almost every question that matters to an asset manager already sits in the documents. The information already exists, but every question turns into a project: open twelve PDFs, reconcile three Excel files, ask a colleague, wait. That is the part nobody has time for, so the question gets answered from memory, from the last version of the spreadsheet, or not at all.
Sometimes the documents disagree with each other. Someone finds out eventually. The only question is whether it is you or someone across the table.

Not catching these issues before they materialize can go unnoticed for months, and then cost a fortune: A notice deadline that nobody diarized, a covenant that turns up during due diligence instead of before it, or a letting strategy that reaches the bank with the business plan and the lease quietly contradicting each other. The bank is the last reader who should catch that. Each of these is a risk or a rent gap that becomes visible only after it has hit the P&L.
None of that is a knowledge problem. It is a reading problem. These documents get read once, if at all, and almost never twice.
Primefold RI reads all of them, every time.
It's live now, and it was built to grow asset value.

Primefold RI brings your entire portfolio into one view. You ask in plain language, RI reads the documents in full context and hands back the analysis with every figure and clause traceable to its source. It connects to your document stack as it is today. Everything stays in your workspace, and we do not use your data to train AI models.
One distinction matters more than any feature: RI is not a search tool that gives you documents. RI gives you answers, with the clause and the page behind it.
The thought process behind RI is simple: Ask. Understand. Act.

Ask where re-letting risk is concentrated and RI reads the leases, amendments and rent rolls that bear on it. Ask which notice deadlines fall in the next twelve months and you get the dates with the clauses that set them. Ask which tenants carry the most lease risk and you get a portfolio view built from the leases themselves, not from a summary somebody typed a year ago.
What RI takes on, in a nutshell:
→ Data validation, such as the rent roll against the leases
→ Lease abstraction, break and notice tracking, covenant monitoring

Documents contradict each other, and a system that hides that is worse than useless. So RI does not smooth it over. Where an extraction is uncertain, it is flagged for review rather than presented as settled, because a number you cannot check is not an answer. If something is missing or does not add up, RI says what it needs. Findings, never a dead end.

It also learns how your house works. Your definition of WALT is not the neighbor's. Your risk thresholds, your document naming, the way you underwrite. RI learns those the first time you correct them and applies them to every deal after that.
NAS Invest, the Frankfurt-based real estate investment firm, put RI on a live portfolio.

A 300-page commercial lease was read and understood in less than an hour. By hand, the team estimates, this would have taken days. The result that mattered even more: two inconsistencies were caught before the letting strategy reached the bank. The business plan disagreed with the lease, and the tenant list disagreed with both. Work that had previously taken four people four weeks was done in a week by one person.
If you have been reading this blog for a while, you know Primefold through XI, which answers questions about people and audiences. RI does the same for your portfolio.
Sunday, the AI agent within Primefold, answers in both. Ask in plain language. Sunday hands back the answer and the source. This holds true for both XI and RI.
Both products are hosted in Germany, built to GDPR requirements. Different angles, same standard of proof.
RI is live now, and we onboard one new partner per month. Bring a real business question and one portfolio, and we will underwrite it live.

p: Your customers were always willing to share. Their checkout page was not.

A customer who has just bought is the easiest person in your business to talk to. They have already decided, they have nothing left to do and they are still looking at your store; the perfect time to ask them about their opinion. But there are obstacles.

The Thank you-page belongs to the checkout, and the checkout belongs to the theme. So asking one question there required a developer, a theme edit and a deploy. The survey went on the list and stayed there.

Earlier this month we shipped Primefold XI · Checkout Survey on the Shopify App Store. The integration lets you add a survey on the post-checkout page without touching a line of theme code. It also asks on every order, not on a list of people who opted into a newsletter three weeks ago. That is the difference between a survey you remember to run and one that runs. h1: We rebuilt our website primefold.ai. Here’s what changed when RI went live.
h2: The part that was harder than it looks
The second reader is an LLM
Ask your data. Get the answer.
p: A website is a map of the company behind it. Ours had one product on it.

In March we changed our name from Saypien to Primefold. Last week, we launched a second intelligence: RI. The website had to catch up with both, and that turned out to be a much more complex challenge than a redesign.

Experience Intelligence is built for marketing, customer experience, product and HR teams. They arrive with a specific question: why NPS dropped in DACH last quarter, or which accounts are showing churn signals right now. They can answer it themselves, and what they want first is a way in.

Real Estate Intelligence is built for asset managers, investment teams and property managers. RI is not self-serve: there is no trial to start on your own, so every partnership begins with a conversation. What they need to see from the product is evidence that an answer can be traced back to the document it came from.

Same company, opposite journeys. One can start today and wants the fastest way in. The other cannot start alone, so the page has to earn a conversation instead. Some readers end up being both: NAS Invest runs XI and RI.
One platform, two intelligences and no page pretending to serve both readers at once.

Each intelligence has its own page now, in its own words. XI talks about surveys, responses and the channels you already use. RI talks about leases, rent rolls, covenants and the clause behind every answer. Neither page borrows the other's vocabulary, because a reader who gets lost in translation is a reader who leaves.

That decision shows up most clearly in the buttons. XI has the option to directly start a trial on your own. RI does not: we onboard one new partner per month, and every new partnership begins with a conversation. A shared button reading "get started" would therefore tell half our readers something untrue about what happens next. So every call to action names the door it opens. Start a trial, or book a call. Worth noting: you can also book a call for XI first if you are interested in the business or enterprise plan right away.

Security, plans, the company pages and this blog stay shared, because both audiences read them, sometimes in the same session. Those pages carry only what is true of the whole platform: where data is stored, what we do and do not do with it, and what you are actually buying.
When you build a second product page, the fastest way to start is from the first one. The structure carries over cleanly. The vocabulary does not.

Respondents, surveys, channels and touchpoints belong to XI. Leases, clauses, rent rolls, covenants and capex schedules belong to RI. A survey has respondents. A portfolio has none. Left alone, a second page inherits the first page's furniture and ends up describing a product that does not exist.

So the nouns are assigned. Each intelligence owns its specific set; shared pages take a neutral set that belongs to neither and every claim on the site has to be traceable to something we can show. A written standard governs all of that, and that is the reason the two intelligences stay distinct as the site grows rather than slowly merging into one blurry thing.

A growing share of business research now starts inside an AI answer rather than on a results page, and that happens whether you want it to or not. Just try to google anything right now and an AI summary will almost always sit above the search results, no matter how you phrase the question. Someone asks which tools read commercial leases, and what comes back is a summary assembled from pages like ours. We are an AI-first company, so this is not a side issue for us. Everything we publish has to work for two readers at once: the person and the machine that will summarize it for them.

That changes what a page has to be good at. An AI model will not read between the lines. It repeats what is explicit. So the pages state plainly what each intelligence does, who it is for, what it costs, where the data sits and what the limits are.
The useful part is that this pulls in the same direction as writing for people. Both readers want the claim and the basis for it in the same place. One of them just refuses to guess.

The whole website, including two product pages. One per intelligence, each in its own language. Case studies with real figures and the basis stated next to them. A security page that says where documents are stored and what happens to them. A plans page that states what is included at each tier. And this blog, where we publish the thinking behind the decisions.
The map matches the company now. Two intelligences, one platform and a core standard behind every sentence on it.
If you want to see either one working with your own material: XI has a trial you can start today. For RI, get in touch with us and we’ll guide you through it.

h1: Primefold XI now speaks German, so does Sunday.
h2: Ask in German, about answers in English
Your survey can be German too
Ask your data. Get the answer.
p: The person who most needs to read what your customers say is not always the person most comfortable reading it in English.

That is the quiet reason research tools lose their audience inside a German company. Whoever bought the tool is fine in English. So is the analyst. But the service lead answering the tickets, the store manager hearing the complaints at the counter and the HR colleague running the engagement survey are all working a language away from the thing they know best, and precision is the entire point of the exercise.
Nobody says the tool is ‘too English’. They just open it less.
That’s why Primefold XI is now available in German.

Go to Settings, then Personal settings, then App language. Choose Deutsch. The app changes as you let go of the mouse: no save, no reload, no confirmation you have to dismiss. What changes is the whole app rather than the navigation bar, down to the error pages and the labels a screen reader reads out.

The part worth noticing is where that setting lives. It sits under Personal rather than under Workspace, next to whether you prefer the light or the dark theme. It belongs to your account, not your workspace. So a team does not have to agree on a language. Two colleagues can work side by side in the same workspace, one with the app in German and one in English. The surveys and the responses stay in whatever language they were written in, shared by both. What follows each person is the interface around the data, not the data itself.

That is a small architectural decision with a large effect on adoption, because the alternative, standardizing a whole company on one working language, is a decision nobody should have to make in order to run a survey.
Sunday answers in German once the setting is German.

More usefully, the language you work in and the language your data is in are two separate entities now. Ask in German about a survey written in English and the answer comes back in German, with the themes named in German and a term like Net Promoter Score left in the form your industry actually uses.
Ask, in any language, which of your questions is the weakest and you get a reason rather than a ranking, then a proposal and a question about whether to apply it, before anything changes.

None of this is translated after the fact. An answer that did not exist until you asked for it has no German version waiting in a file somewhere. Sunday writes it in German, which is why your data can stay in one language while you work in another.

This does not stop at the interface you work in. Ask Sunday for a survey in German, or simply write the request in German, and the questions come back in German. A German team can run German research without drafting anything twice.

There is one limit worth knowing. A survey runs in the language it was built in, so respondents see the language you created it in: a German survey goes out in German, an English one in English. Serving the same survey to each respondent in their own language is not there yet.
So the language choice is yours twice over. Once for the room you work in, and once for every survey you build.

Primefold is a German company, so are many of the companies we work with. That is why a rough translation was never an option. Engineers, product and customer-facing colleagues went through the terms one by one, and the result was finalized by a professional translator. Some words stayed in English on purpose: the Insights Hub is a named surface, not a description.
Switching the language takes no more than a few clicks and applies to you alone, so you can try it without asking anyone.

The survey went up as stickers inside the lifts, set so the sticker is what you look at once the doors close, and went out by email at the same time. What would have taken four weeks and four people was done in a week, by a single person.

Customers in the first year, with Primefold XI making an impact.

Gainback gives restaurants, hotels and local businesses the marketing tools that used to belong to large chains: digital stamp cards, loyalty programs, giveaways and surveys. The company that sells clarity about customers had none about its own market: who exactly buys, what the market wants and why anyone stays.

At this stage, a wrong answer costs runway. Demo calls, onboarding conversations, support messages, feature requests, usage patterns, the reason behind every deal won and lost, each one carried a clue. None of them added up to a picture, and there was no research team, no capacity for the manual work of reading it all and no time to build either.

Nobody at Gainback had done this before. There was no research function to inherit and no budget to hire someone, so the real choice was between deciding on instinct and building the system while still selling. For a large company, customer intelligence is an optimization project. For a startup it is navigation. Now every theme in a report keeps the responses behind it, so a claim about the market traces back to the customer who made it.Selling a product built on loyalty is supposed to mean knowing why people come back. For a team whose evidence lived in five inboxes and two founders' heads, that knowledge stopped at whoever happened to remember it.

Gainback partnered with Primefold early, before there was much of a customer base to survey. The rollout took the customer journey as it already existed and gave every stage of it a place to answer: the first demo, the onboarding check-in, regular strategy calls, in-product flows, automated surveys, support follow-ups and the moment a customer renews or leaves.

The human touchpoints turn conversations that used to evaporate into recorded, analyzable signal. The digital ones sit inside Gainback's own stack, so the implementation left nobody a new tool to log into, and the automation collects whether anyone remembers it or not.

Strategy calls run on a fixed cadence, the in-product and support touchpoints are continuous, and all of it lands in Experience Intelligence. Sunday reads the open text and returns themes, sentiment and the strongest drivers in minutes instead of days, and in the voice of the customer. What comes out splits three ways: what to fix in onboarding, what to build next and which segment to sell to.

Because every touchpoint reports into the same view, an answer from a support thread and an answer from a lost deal can be compared rather than argued about. Customer retention became a managed number rather than a hope, and a churn rate you can explain is one you can act on. Growth stops depending on who remembered which conversation.
Who the ideal customer actually was.

Every founder can describe their ideal customer. The description is usually built from the loudest conversations, because that is the evidence within reach. Answers and usage across segments replaced it with an ideal customer profile that holds up: which segments show the fastest adoption, which stay longest and which grow. Sales and marketing now aim at that instead of at the whole market.

Customers said which features created the most value for a café or a hotel, where onboarding produced friction and which use cases turned a trial into a customer who stays. That went straight into the roadmap, including new digital products that exist because the data asked for them. Product-market fit is easier to find when the market keeps telling you where it is.

Gainback's own product produces loyalty and engagement data for the businesses that run it. With that data in one place, the team can show a prospect what the product did for businesses like theirs, in numbers rather than in promises. Most companies this young have a deck instead.
